system:
You are the Arabic language reviewer, standing in for an Arabic reviewer at the issuing authority. You compare the Arabic text with the English text and report any difference in meaning: numbers, times, places, the hazard, and above all the protective action. You cannot approve the Arabic; a named person who reads Arabic still must.
You see only the English and Arabic headline, description and instruction, and how the Arabic was produced. You cannot approve or send the alert; people decide.

Review the alert within your mandate only. Decide:
- "agree": nothing within your mandate is wrong;
- "object": something is wrong and the drafter can fix it (say how in `fix`);
- "escalate": something is wrong that needs a decision by a person or a higher authority.

Every objection needs evidence. Each evidence item is a word-for-word quote (at least 5 words for a
clause, at least 3 for the alert or inputs) from either a knowledge base clause shown to you (kind
"clause", ref = its id) or the material you were shown (kind "view", ref = the field name). Quotes are
checked by code; an objection with no quote that matches is thrown away. Do not object to things
outside your mandate. Do not repeat the same issue twice.
If you have a concern but none of the clauses shown supports it, put it in `no_basis` instead.

When automated language translation of free form text content in an <info> block has taken place, a single instance of this parameter should be used with a value of “yes”.

[CAPCP#0080] Canadian Profile of the Common Alerting Protocol (CAP-CP): Introduction and Rule Set 1.0 (Draft 2) (Rule #5. <info> blocks must specify the content language):
Multilingual messages must use separate <info> blocks for each language, with all non free-form text elements repeated verbatim in each block. Mixing public display content or text from different languages within the same <info> block is not allowed, except for inherently multilingual content (people, places, things) that may or may not include accented characters.

data.summary: The Arabic text matches the English in meaning. The hazard (rain, heavy at times), the areas (some eastern, southern, western and interior areas), the date and time (Sat 22 Aug, 13:30-21:00) and the protective action (drive with care, follow updates) all match, with no differences in numbers, times, places or action. One non-blocking issue: the sender acronym 'NCM' is left in Latin script three times in the Arabic text, which Arabic-only readers may not recognise. The Arabic was produced by machine translation, so a named person who reads Arabic must still review and approve it before it is sent; this review does not approve it.

objections.issue: The Arabic headline, description and instruction keep the English acronym 'NCM' in Latin script instead of naming the issuing authority in Arabic. This mixes languages in the Arabic public display text, and Arabic-only recipients may not recognise who issued the alert. The meaning is otherwise unchanged.
objections.fix: Replace 'NCM' in the Arabic text with the authority's official Arabic name, for example 'المركز الوطني للأرصاد'. Examples: 'تنبيه أمطار من المركز الوطني للأرصاد', 'المركز الوطني للأرصاد: أمطار...', 'تابع تحديثات المركز الوطني للأرصاد'. The Arabic reviewer should confirm the exact official Arabic name.

evidence.quote: Mixing public display content or text from different languages within the same <info> block is not allowed

no_basis.concern: The imperative 'قُد بحذر' is in the masculine singular form. That is common in Arabic public messaging, but the human reviewer may prefer a gender-neutral wording such as 'يُرجى القيادة بحذر'. This is a style matter, not a difference in meaning.
